title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.The move comes after trade talks be
body: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter-tariffs next month.Trump said the renaming of the lake, which straddles both countries, was effective immediately. He has broad discretion over how the US recognises landmarks but other countries do not have to follow.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in response that "things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever".The executive order gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.Carney noted that the name Lake Ontario could be traced back more than 400 years, adding that it preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence."We know that the United States is changing," he said. "Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms."Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario - today and forever."There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters.When Trump took to the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water. It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application., externalIn that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)". The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.There was a mixed reaction from US politicians.Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing: "We're on it, Mr. President!""The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".But Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic". She wrote: "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect". Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, would not be calling it Lake America.

schema.headline: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America

title: Rwanda genocide: Dutch court sentences man to life over massacre
description: A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.The 66-year-old, named only as
body: A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said. Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen.In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists.The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda."The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes".At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them.Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said.Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire."Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said.As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024.N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events"."The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide.His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP.

schema.headline: Rwanda genocide: Dutch court sentences man to life over massacre

title: Uganda's King Oyo: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
description: The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch. Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown i
body: The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch. Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured"."His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, The Denver Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, When he was 10, King Oyo was pictured on a trip to the US with Queen Mother Best Kemigisa (L) and Mayor of the city of Denver Wellington Webb (R). He was there on a humanitarian mission for Aids orphans in Uganda.Slide 1 of 3, 10-year-old King Oyo of the Kingdom of Toro in Africa, second from left, eyes Denver Mayor Wellington Webb, right, during an introductory meeting with the King's mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Olimi, far left; and Denver First Lady Wilma Webb at the Denver City and County building Monday. The King, the youngest monarch in the world, is visiting Denver on a humanitarian mission for AIDS orphans in Uganda, When he was 10, King Oyo was pictured on a trip to the US with Queen Mother Best Kemigisa (L) and Mayor of the city of Denver Wellington Webb (R). He was there on a humanitarian mission for Aids orphans in Uganda.

title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge says
description: A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk,
body: A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless".The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for tasks including surveillance or autonomous weapons.US District Judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security was "not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics".Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment.Anthropic was focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology", a spokesperson told the BBC.Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic.The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such.Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful".The Claude maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights. The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action. The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service".The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology.Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated.Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI."This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added.

schema.headline: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge says

title: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health
description: An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation.Jerusale
body: An Israeli court has acquitted a Jewish man who attacked a nun in Jerusalem, in an incident caught on CCTV which drew widespread condemnation.Jerusalem Magistrates Court said Yona Schreiber was experiencing a psychotic episode when he pushed over and kicked the French nun in the Old City in occupied East Jerusalem in April. It ruled that he was not criminally responsible for his actions and ordered him to be sent to a psychiatric hospital for up to six years.Video of the attack caused outrage, and deepened concerns after a rise in harassment of Christian clergy and pilgrims by Jewish extremists in the Old City.The victim, who hit her head on a stone block, suffered a bruised face and leg.Schreiber, 36, had been charged with assault motivated by hostility towards a religious group.According to the district psychiatrist's report, Schreiber "was in a psychotic state at the time of the act and is not substantively fit to stand trial". The prosecution accepted the psychiatrist's opinion and asked for Schreiber to be acquitted and committed to hospital.Judge Ofir Tishler said that although Schrieber had attacked the nun, he was ordering his acquittal due to his mental health.At the time of the attack, the French Consulate in Jerusalem said it strongly condemned Schreiber's "aggression".The director of the French Biblical and Archaeological School, where the nun is a researcher, called the assault an "act of sectarian violence".Israel's foreign ministry denounced the attack, calling it a "shameful act [which] stands in direct contradiction to the values of respect, coexistence, and religious freedom upon which Israel is founded and to which it remains deeply committed.""Israel remains firmly committed to safeguarding freedom of religion and freedom of worship for all faiths, and to ensuring that Jerusalem remains a city where every community can live, pray, and practice its faith in safety and dignity," the ministry said on X.While the violence of the attack on the nun is unusual, in the past few years in Jerusalem's Old City there have been regular cases of religious Jews spitting and acting aggressively towards those wearing Christian religious dress or symbols.Church properties have been vandalised and there have also been bitter disputes caused by settler takeovers. Church leaders accuse Israel of trying to change the status quo – long-standing agreements on ownership and responsibilities - at their holy places.A 2025 report by the Rossing Center, a Jerusalem-based organisation which aims to foster better inter-faith relations in the Holy Land, describes a "recent surge in overt animosity towards Christianity", putting this down to "a continued deepening of polarisation and ultra-nationalist political trends".

schema.headline: Man who attacked nun on CCTV in Jerusalem acquitted on grounds of mental health

title: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: These two women are among nearly 300 Indians missing
description: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stoppedImage source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, S
body: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stoppedImage source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimageByIndia correspondentEarly on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years. Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message."After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.Image source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement. In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square. She told her husband the countryside was beautiful."She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night. She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one. A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.There was little to suggest what was coming.Image source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck."I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since."Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards."Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border regionFor the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu."She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family."She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said. The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina  outside the Nepal immigration centre.Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.Image source, Dwaipayan MukherjeeImage caption, Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says.  "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains. Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list , externalof 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

schema.headline: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: These two women are among nearly 300 Indians missing

title: Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, King Haakon VIII has adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway"ByJames Gregory and Mallory MoenchKing
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, King Haakon VIII has adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway"ByJames Gregory and Mallory MoenchKing Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent."I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected. "King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother."But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, At the age of 22, Ingrid Alexandra becomes Norway's crown princessHaakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession. The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century.Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family.The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook. But in recent years it has been beset by scandal. Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction.Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja.By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years. "Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... ​At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s. He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V.Image source, EPAImage caption, Three generations of monarch at the family's Skaugum estate in 1982 - King Olav V, with the young Prince Haakon and then-Crown Prince HaraldUnusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995.He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science.Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999.She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings."What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001.But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession. Image source, EPAImage caption, Crown Princess Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, Prince Haakon and Crown Prince Harald at Skaugum in 1987The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either. What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s. She did not say whether she had taken them herself.It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Haakon and Mette-Marit married in August 2001In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy. Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview  that she wished she had never met him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Haakon's family affairs have been the subject of media and public scrutiny in recent timesSeveral polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis. Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own". "But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says. "What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task"."I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.

schema.headline: Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII?

title: 'Not far enough' - parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
description: For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more
body: For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers.But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term."It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says.This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children.The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters.It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained.Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make.Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters.But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving"."People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that."Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers."Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it."Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms".Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem."They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing."Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night."I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?"The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault.The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information.The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms.For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic.Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms.The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements.It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty"."That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says.Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says.

schema.headline: 'Not far enough' - parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users

title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises
description: Figure caption, Watch: A look back at the King who broke with traditionByMallory MoenchUpdated 6 hours agoNorway's King Harald V has died at the age o
body: Figure caption, Watch: A look back at the King who broke with traditionByMallory MoenchUpdated 6 hours agoNorway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition.The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo. The royal flag on the roof of the palace has been lowered to half-mast and a period of national mourning has been declared leading up to the day of his funeral. Crowds of mourners have streamed to the royal palace to lay flowers and flags.Harald was the nation's first king born there since the 14th Century. He has been succeeded by his son Haakon, 53, who will hold an extraordinary council of state with the government later on Friday.Image source, Anwar Hussein/Getty ImagesImage caption, Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th CenturyKing Charles III sent his "most heartfelt condolences" at the death of his "dear cousin" - who was a second cousin to Queen Elizabeth II - while King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden remembered "a good friend to me, my family and to Sweden", wishing his godson Haakon "success and good fortune".After 35 years on the throne, Harald will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments.Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V.During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent about the royal family's finances and health matters, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC.Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people"."He has never been afraid to show emotion, humour or vulnerability, and that has made him very human."Image source, REUTERS/Dylan MartinezIn the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over".More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape.He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren.In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over".More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape.He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren.Image source, Dominic Lipinski/PA WireImage caption, King Harald and Queen Elizabeth II were second cousins Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered the Nazi German invasion of Norway early in World War Two.Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt.Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, studying social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962.He met Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald once told Norway's public broadcaster, external.His father finally gave his consent and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated royal family".Image source, Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesImage caption, (L-R) Prince Sverre Magnus, the new King Haakon, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja and King Harald of Norway attend Norwegian Constitution Day at the Royal Palace in Oslo in MayWhen his father became ill in 1990, the then-crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991.The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a shy man into someone much more open and empathetic.In July 2011, Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving onto a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers.He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke."I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As king of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said.Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesIn 2016, the king made headlines again by giving a, external speech, external supporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation.He said Norwegians were from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia and Syria", that they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and that they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other".The king was also a keen athlete and environmentalist - one of the initiators of the Norwegian branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who served as president of the Norwegian chapter for 20 years.He was such an accomplished sailor, he represented Norway three times at the Olympics.When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed that he was never a royal.The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties.Image source, NTB/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, King Harald welcomed the Norwegian national football team to the palace after they made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup for the first time this yearWhile some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions".As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024. More recently, he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, assuming his activities.This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals.The rape trial of Høiby, convicted of multiple offences in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died. Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Harald and Sonja regularly supported Norway's teams at the OlympicsShe later apologised to Harald and Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement".Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years prior.Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for newspaper Aftenposten found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%. Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will.However, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald"."When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," Isaksen remarked.Haakon has faced questions about the turbulence surrounding his own household that will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well. The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Høiby's trial, and Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded.Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

schema.headline: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises

title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
description: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandHenry Moore and Amy WalkerUpdated 1 hour agoDevastating lan
body: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandHenry Moore and Amy WalkerUpdated 1 hour agoDevastating landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.At least 547 people have been killed and 977 people remain unaccounted for two days after floodwaters tore through the border region, sweeping away homes and roads, local officials have said.Rescue workers say they now face a critical moment to reach remaining survivors as fears mount of further flooding in the disaster's aftermath.Here is what we know so far.What caused the landslide?Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating floods early on Wednesday.However, the US Geological Survey (USGS) later confirmed that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse" - when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency, causing "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream".Powerful floodwaters and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km) downstream from the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi Rivers, the USGS said, sweeping through towns popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims in northern Nepal.Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles as people fled in the Nuwakot region.In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuwagadhi Border checkpoint, a multi-storey building on the Nepalese side. Gyirong Port, over the border, was also hit. A number of deaths were reported in Tibetan villages.Scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events as rescue efforts continue. Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet."I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, [which] dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood," he told the BBC.Figure caption, Watch: What caused the Nepal-Tibet flash floods?The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of debris that washed into the river systems.The ICIDMOD said it was assessing whether the Trishuli River had been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If this is the case, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam and a second flood.Separately, China has warned there was a "high risk" a lake that formed after the landslide may burst its banks, causing fresh flooding downstream. As of Friday, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated, according to broadcaster CCTV. State media reported that rescue operations were briefly suspended on Friday after the lake, which has formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, overflowed - before water levels dropped slightly. Heavy rain is forecast over the next few days.But experts have told the BBC that it was possible that the lake could drain naturally over time. Figure caption, Watch: The lake prompting fears of second flood in NepalHow many people are dead and missing?The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear.At least 547 people had died as of Friday, according to Nepali police, while the country's disaster agency said 977 people were still missing.The government has released a list of more than 500 foreign nationals who have been out of contact since the floods hit, including 33 UK nationals. The missing also include 44 members of the Nepali army and 28 police officers, disaster officials have said.Meanwhile, five people have died in Tibet and 558 are missing, China's state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday.It is unclear whether any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, a spokesman for Nepal's army, told the BBC that rain and unpredictable weather in the area were making rescue operations increasingly challenging.Which countries are the missing tourists from?Figure caption, Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet borderTourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Reports of those missing include the following:India - Nepal's tourism board says 178 nationals from neighbouring India are missingChina - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in NepalUS - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missingUkraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missingMalaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials sayAustralia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will riseUK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missingCanada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missingSmaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.How are governments responding?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police officers were pictured carrying a survivor from the flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot districtAs rescue operations continued on Friday, the office of Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "additional" personnel were on the ground to speed up recovery efforts.It added that a 1,200-strong team has been deployed "along the riverbanks from Rasuwa to Chitwan" and "to all possible locations along the affected areas".Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting of officials to co-ordinate rescue efforts, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.Kamal Kishore, special representative of the UN secretary general for disaster risk reduction, urged countries to support response efforts.The US previously promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid for communities affected by the floods, while the UK said it had offered £5m.Meanwhile, the Indian Air Force said that military cargo planes carrying nearly 50 tonnes of supplies had been sent to Nepal.Might climate change have played a role?Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.Geologist Daniel Shugar – one of the first experts to suggest Wednesday's flash flooding could have been caused by glacial activity – said glacial thinning caused by global warming could increase the risk of landslides.But it is still too early to definitively link the event to climate change, Shugar, who is based at the University of Calgary in Canada, told the BBC.Simon Cook, a geoscientist at the University of Dundee, said that climate change "could have an impact".He said his team believed they had identified where the collapse had occurred. He told the BBC that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - approximately 15km west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.Cook estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.He told the BBC that "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".

schema.headline: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods

title: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions
description: A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the
body: A senior official on US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of the Palestinian armed group Hamas.Nickolay Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.He was speaking to the UN Security Council after Israel rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament, which was announced by the Board of Peace last month.Hamas has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal. But Israel has insisted that the group must fully disarm before any pullout.At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.The Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza told the Security Council on Wednesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed at their last meeting on a mechanism through which his government's remaining questions would be settled and that committees had been established for that purpose.Mladenov said that process had not stalled but warned that risks remained, including the continued killing of Palestinian civilians in Israeli strikes."A ceasefire in fact under which civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel. Every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat, and every incident that the deconfliction mechanism was not asked to resolve, costs this process something very hard to buy back," he added.Mladenov acknowledged that Hamas too had yet to meet fully its commitment to cease all military activities."Every weapon carried, every tunnel still worked and every convoy still obstructed sets the process back and hands an argument to those who want to resume war," he said.He repeated that under the new roadmap, Israeli troop withdrawal from Gaza "follows verified decommissioning" of Hamas weapons handed over to the Palestinian technocratic committee that will govern Gaza under the Board of Peace's supervision."It is sequenced and reciprocal," he said.That is a key difference from comments made by President Trump's envoy, Jared Kushner, after meeting Israel's prime minister two weeks ago.He said Israeli withdrawal would be discussed only once the demilitarisation of Gaza was "done" - appearing to change the plan in line with Israel's demands.Israel's representative told the Security Council meeting that it was committed to last October's US-brokered plan for ending the Gaza war, but she insisted it could not succeed while Hamas still had weapons, tunnels and other military infrastructure."Disarmament must come first," she stated.The Palestinian representative said Israel was killing Palestinian civilians with impunity in Gaza and called on the international community to protect them without delay.Mladenov warned that if the ceasefire was allowed to collapse, "there will be no roadmap to return to, there will be no administration to deploy, and there will be nothing left of the ground to rebuild"."That would not be a setback. It would be a point of no return for everyone."The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,430 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

schema.headline: Board of Peace's Gaza envoy criticises Israeli strikes and Hamas actions

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
description: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.At least 469 people have died a
body: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.At least 469 people have died and several hundred others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake.Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas."My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC.Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster."They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how."Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand.He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable."I am worried she must be swept away."Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle."My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left."At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates.Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday."But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC.Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend."I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said.Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time.As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village."It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo."Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members.He described the flood as "sudden and devastating"."Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support."He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away

title: Tate brothers condemn US jail conditions as they await possible UK extradition
description: Andrew and Tristan Tate have told a Florida court they should be released from jail so they can fight extradition to the UK on charges of rape and tra
body: Andrew and Tristan Tate have told a Florida court they should be released from jail so they can fight extradition to the UK on charges of rape and trafficking.Wearing tan jail uniforms, the brothers maintained they did not commit the alleged crimes as they hit out at conditions in US custody.Government lawyers argued that the two were a flight risk and had bragged about having multiple passports, while defence attorneys said the two social media influencers' high profile would make it almost impossible for them to flee.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis will issue a written ruling at a later date on whether to grant bail to the dual British-US citizens. The two were arrested in Miami on 19 July.During Thursday's hearing, defence lawyers said the pair had complied with the terms of their release while they battled the UK charges and another case in Romania.US authorities took the men into custody last month after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled dozens of new charges against them.The British authorities have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request.The brothers, who arrived in court in shackles, were questioned in turn by their defence attorneys and government lawyers as they took the stand.Andrew Tate, 39, declared he has "never committed the crimes I'm accused of".Tristan Tate, 38, described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little sunlight and exercise."It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he told the court, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner."It's death by scurvy," he said, adding that he had lost 14lb (6.3kg).The British Embassy filed court documents asking the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK pursues extradition.US government lawyers pushed back against the brothers' claims that they had exaggerated their wealth to massage their online personas.The federal attorneys said the Tates had access to resources that could help fund an escape and they had bragged about having multiple passports.But Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer, testified that to support himself financially, he "had to go back to the boxing ring against heavier, younger opponents", according to CBS News."I've said some stupid things, but sometimes you have to shake the internet to get noticed," he testified about his online statements, according to CBS."This is the reality of the internet."I'm being treated like El Chapo," he added, referring to the Mexican drug kingpin, "but I have a perfect record in the court system".Under questioning from his attorney, Joseph McBride, Andrew Tate denied he was a human trafficker.The defence also called Natasha Sesay, from England, to testify in support of releasing Andrew Tate.She described a five-year romantic relationship, saying she had had one child with him and was expecting a second."It's nice having him at home," she told the court, reports CBS.Sesay also said that despite his online persona, Andrew Tate "has never ever been violent toward women", according to CBS.The UK has brought a total of 59 criminal charges against the Tates, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.The British authorities filed 21 charges last year against the brothers, then 38 additional counts last month.The combined charges involve seven accusers, UK prosecutors said.The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025."If I go to England they will lock me up," Tristan Tate said on the stand in Miami on Thursday, "and take everything I've ever worked for".He also said the Romanian charges had "destroyed my entire life", reports CBS."They took everything, even the savings accounts for their [his children's] college funds. This case is make or break for me."The Tates built an influencer empire in the so-called manosphere, showcasing a lifestyle of conspicuous wealth and excess.Andrew Tate accumulated millions of followers among an audience of primarily young men.The White House has said President Donald Trump will not intervene in the extradition case of the brothers, who have been vocal supporters of him.

schema.headline: Tate brothers condemn US jail conditions as they await possible UK extradition

title: Shootings surge as drug gangs torment Brussels
description: Image source, EPAByBruno BoelpaepReporting fromBrusselsLast Monday night, drug gangs turned Salvatore's pizzeria in Brussels into a crime scene."We dr
body: Image source, EPAByBruno BoelpaepReporting fromBrusselsLast Monday night, drug gangs turned Salvatore's pizzeria in Brussels into a crime scene."We dropped to the floor. I had clients eating on the terrace with children. Look, we can see the bullet impacts everywhere."His restaurant sits on a pretty little square in St Gilles. It's a central area of the city, close to the international Midi train station, where passengers arrive on trains from London and Paris.Shootings related to drug trafficking have become routine in the Belgian capital over the past couple of years. There were over 100 in 2025 alone, and more than 65 shootings so far this year.This was the third shooting in this neighbourhood in just three days."Are we in an American gangster movie? This needs to stop," Salvatore says.Image caption, "Are we in an American gangster movie? This needs to stop," says Salvatore, after a shooting at his Brussels pizzeriaA suspected drug dealer was shot in the leg in the same area the day before. Now Murielle and her dog Chéva are sitting at that exact spot, just across the street: "We can still see the trace of the pool of blood."Murielle is 70, and hopes peace soon returns to her street."I like it here. It's like a little village inside the city. Even the drug dealers used to be polite and decent. I would just tell them to go further away and they'd say, 'Yes, ok mama!'"Image caption, Murielle says the drug dealers used to be polite in this part of the city - but not any moreDrug dealing is happening in plain sight here. Only five minutes after I arrive, I witness a transaction.A buyer walks up to the seller, shakes their hand, and walks away with the drugs. Crack has become widely consumed amongst the poorest in this area of Brussels."Things have changed in the past six months," says Murielle. "The business has intensified. Sometimes you even see consumers queuing to buy drugs. And now gangs are fighting over this spot."A successful drug-dealing point in Brussels nets up to €50,000 ($58,000; £43,000) per day or more for the dealer, according to the chief of Brussels South Police, Jurgen de Landsheer.Organised crime in the Belgian capital has become significantly more violent, he says.At the heart of it all is money. There are more than 200 drug-dealing points across the city, according to the police.The rise of drug-related violence in the Belgian capital echoes the situation of other European cities such as the French port of Marseille. Cocaine has become widely available in Europe,  the continent's ports serving as entry points for the drug. The port of Antwerp, just 40km (25 miles) away, has seen record cocaine seizures in recent years.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Antwerp has seen record seizures on drugs in recent yearsJurgen de Landsheer says gangs in Brussels are now adopting methods seen in Marseille, although he insists his city has not reached the same level of violence."We don't have no-go zones here in Brussels. It's not easy to go in some neighbourhoods, but we go everywhere. We don't want to become like some neighbourhoods in Marseille, so we'll do everything to stop it."A police station even came under attack last weekend.CCTV footage shows two men on a scooter stopping in front of the building and shooting at the door several times with what looks like an AK-47 before leaving on their scooter.This marks an escalation, as it is the first time criminals have targeted police. Usually, the shootings involve rival gangs."We see a lot of young people getting paid a few hundred euros. They get a weapon, AK-47 or other heavy weapon, and then they get a mission. To shoot a person in the leg, for example, or to try to kill somebody. And they get very little money for this."De Landsheer says some of the people his men arrest are as young as 12, and that makes it very dangerous for the whole community."The biggest danger is a stray bullet."BBCThere is no magic solution. We need prevention over repressionThe spike in shootings has forced Belgian authorities to react and, on Thursday, Belgium's interior minister announced that an extra 40 police officers would be deployed in the problem area.Jurgen de Landsheer is aware that police alone will not solve this crisis."There is no magic solution. We need prevention over repression. We can do our part and be present in the street, but our society also needs to give a future to the young people, do something with them. That's the social part."Back in St Gilles, Salvatore says it's time for the violence to end."Nobody sleeps here at the moment. People talk about moving out, houses are losing value."Murielle wants to believe that the worst is now behind."We will not be intimidated. We'll carry on living and we'll keep on protecting our lovely neighbourhood."

schema.headline: Shootings surge as drug gangs torment Brussels

title: Norway King Harald: A look back at the King who broke with tradition
description: Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89 after he was taken to hospital for treatment for a rare blood condition.The palace in Oslo said he pa
body: Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89 after he was taken to hospital for treatment for a rare blood condition.The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35GMT) on Friday at the national hospital.Daniel Sandford takes a look back at his life.Read more on King Harald's life.

schema.headline: Norway King Harald: A look back at the King who broke with tradition
